cities.base: Center, near the bazaar and the road east to Issyk-Kul, purely a landing and departure buffer
cities.name: Bishkek

cities.base: Town center, walkable to guesthouses and gear rental, base for the traverse and staging point both directions
cities.name: Karakol

places.name: Metro Bar
places.note: Long-running expat and local bar, reliable for a beer and decompressing after the flight in or before the flight out.

places.name: Navat
places.note: Central Asian dishes, manti and lagman done well, comfortable sit-down spot for a first or last night dinner without being a tourist trap.

places.name: Victory Square
places.note: Yurt-shaped WWII memorial with an eternal flame. Worth a five-minute stop if walking past, not a destination on its own.

places.name: Frunze House Museum
places.note: Preserved childhood home of the Soviet general the city was once named after. Niche interest only, skip unless you specifically care about Soviet military history.

places.name: Jash Kelin (Osh Plov spot near Jibek Jolu)
places.note: Plov cooked in giant kazans, cheap and filling. Order the plov, nothing else, and eat with the regulars at shared tables.

places.name: Oak Park (Dubovy Park)
places.note: Tree-lined park with Soviet sculptures scattered among the oaks. Quiet, locals walking dogs and playing chess, easy half hour.

places.name: Kyrgyz State Historical Museum
places.note: Soviet-era building on Ala-Too Square with a wild mix of Lenin murals downstairs and nomadic Kyrgyz artifacts upstairs. Good rainy-afternoon option, closed Mondays.

places.name: Ala-Too Square
places.note: The main square, flag changing ceremony on the hour is mildly interesting. Fine to walk through on the way somewhere else, not worth a special trip.

places.name: Osh Bazaar
places.note: Sprawling produce and dried fruit market, this is where people actually shop, not a staged version for tourists. Good for dried fruit and nuts to take on the trek.

places.name: CBT Gear Rental
places.note: Rent the tent, sleeping bag and crampons you didn't want to fly with, sort this the afternoon before you start.

places.name: Fat Boys
places.note: The trekker canteen, reliable comfort food and where you'll find a guide or a ride if you need one.

places.name: Dungan Mosque
places.note: Wooden mosque built without nails, a quick stop before or after the trek, not a whole afternoon.

places.name: Osh Bazaar
places.note: The real city market, good for dried fruit and last-minute trek snacks, not styled for visitors.

places.name: Ala-Too Square
places.note: Soviet-scale plaza worth a walk-through on the way somewhere else, not worth planning around.

places.name: Arashan Bathhouse
places.note: A decent Soviet-era banya to loosen up after the long flight in, cheap and unglamorous.

places.name: Karakol Animal Market
places.note: Sunday-only livestock market, chaotic and real, worth the early start if the day lines up.

places.name: Descent to Altyn Arashan Valley
places.note: Long knee-jarring descent from the lake down into the Altyn Arashan valley, 5 hours or so, dropping through alpine meadow and larch forest. Altyn Arashan itself is a scatter of guesthouses and hot springs at the bottom, a good place to stop for the night rather than pushing straight out to Karakol.

places.name: Karakol Valley Waterfall Walk (low-route alternative)
places.note: The fallback when wind or weather closes the pass. Follows the Karakol river through forest to a waterfall, flat and sheltered by trees most of the way, 3-4 hours round trip. No exposure, no pass, but still gets you into the same valley system. Use this day to wait out weather rather than risk the pass in a storm.

places.name: Altyn Arashan Hot Springs
places.note: Simple concrete pools fed by a natural hot spring, right by the guesthouses at the bottom of the descent. Basic, no frills, exactly what you want on the legs after the pass. Small fee paid to whichever guesthouse runs the pool that season.

places.name: Karakol (Fish) Lake side detour
places.note: Skip. A small lake passed early in the standard route, sometimes hyped in trip reports, but it is a muddy pond by comparison to what is coming, and stopping here just burns daylight needed for the pass.

places.name: Moraine Ridge above Ala-Kul Base Camp
places.note: A short scramble up the moraine behind base camp for a sunset view back down the valley, roughly 30 minutes up. Good use of the hour before dark on the acclimatization night if legs have anything left.

places.name: Karakol National Park Entry Checkpoint
places.note: Where park fees are collected before the trail starts, cash only, small entrance building. Not a sight in itself, just where the trek officially begins and where you will queue briefly with other groups on a summer morning.

places.name: Horse and Gear Portage Service (CBT Karakol)
places.note: Arranged through CBT or a Karakol trekking agency, not a fixed place but worth flagging: paying for a horse to carry the heavy pack up to base camp turns day one from a slog into a walk, and buys back energy for the pass. Given the trip is already time-compressed, this is money well spent.

places.name: Ak-Suu (Teploklyuchenka) Guesthouses
places.note: The village at the base of the trailhead, used as a jump-off point rather than a destination. CBT-run guesthouses here can arrange horses to carry gear up to base camp, which is worth paying for given how little time there is to spare.

places.name: Jyrgalan Village
places.note: Skip for this trip. It is a genuinely good base for other treks and has become the community-tourism darling of the region, but it pulls in the opposite direction from Karakol and Ala-Kul, and there is no spare day to reach it. Worth a separate trip, not this one.

places.name: Day 2: Base Camp to Ala-Kul Pass and the Lake
places.note: Steep scree climb from camp to the pass, 2-3 hours, then a short drop to the lake shore. Ala-Kul itself is turquoise, sits at 3560m, ringed by scree slopes with almost no vegetation. Cold and windy at the pass even in summer, go early before afternoon wind and cloud build up. This is the payoff view of the whole trek.

places.name: Day 1: Ak-Suu Trailhead to Ala-Kul Base Camp
places.note: Trailhead near the Karakol ranger checkpoint past Ak-Suu village, about 18km, 1000m elevation gain, 6-7 hours at a steady pace. Follows the river through forest then opens onto scree and moraine. Most people camp at Ala-Kul base camp around 3200m the night before the pass. Entry fee to Karakol National Park collected at the checkpoint, roughly 150-250 som.

places.name: Ala-Kul to Altyn Arashan Traverse (via Ala-Kul Pass)
places.note: The classic two to three day traverse. Day 1 from Ak-Suu (Arashan) trailhead up the Ak-Suu valley to a camp below the pass, roughly 6-7 hours and 1000m gain. Day 2 is the pass itself, 3860m, then the long descent to Altyn Arashan, another 8-9 hours total. Snow on the pass into June and from October is normal, crampons or microspikes help. This is the whole reason to come here, everything else on this list supports it.

places.name: Przhevalsky Museum and Memorial
places.note: Memorial complex by the lake to the Russian explorer, small museum with dated exhibits and limited English. Skip unless it's raining and you've already done everything else on this list, the setting by Issyk-Kul is nicer than the museum itself.

places.name: Yak Bar & Grill
places.note: Sit-down dinner spot in town serving Kyrgyz staples including yak dishes, plov and manty. Good post-trek meal, portions are large, service is slow.

places.name: Ashlyan-Fu Stalls (Karakol style)
places.note: Cold spicy noodle and starch-jelly soup, a Dungan dish specific to this region, sold from small stalls and cafes around town rather than one single address. Cheap, fast, and the thing to eat here that you won't find elsewhere in the country.

places.name: Fabrika Coffee & Kitchen
places.note: Reliable sit-down breakfast and decent coffee in a town where good espresso is not a given, useful the morning you're packing to head up the valley.

places.name: Karakol Ski Base
places.note: Small ski resort about 6km above town with a chairlift running in summer too, decent views over the valley without any hiking required. Only worth it if the trek is weathered out and you want to still get up high, otherwise skip in favor of the actual trek days.

places.name: Karakol Central Bazaar
places.note: Everyday town market, useful for stocking up on trail snacks, dried fruit, bread and cheap gear before the trek rather than for sightseeing.

places.name: Karakol Animal Market (Mal Bazaar)
places.note: Sunday mornings only, on the edge of town. Farmers trading sheep, cattle and horses, loud and genuinely working, not staged for visitors. Go early, it winds down by mid-morning and it smells exactly like you'd expect.

places.name: Holy Trinity Cathedral
places.note: Russian Orthodox wooden cathedral, bright blue and white, originally built in the 1890s and rebuilt after an earthquake. Sits in a park, five minutes if you're not going in, pair it with the Dungan Mosque since they're a short walk apart.

places.name: Dungan Mosque
places.note: Wooden mosque built in 1910 without a single nail, Chinese pagoda style rather than the usual dome and minaret. Small, take ten minutes, worth the short stop between other errands in town.

places.name: Altyn Arashan Hot Springs
places.note: Basic wooden tubs fed by a natural hot spring at the end of the traverse, exactly what you want after the Ala-Kul pass. Not a resort, expect rustic guesthouse-run pools, sometimes cold by the time you get there if a group beat you to it.

places.name: Jeti-Oguz (Seven Bulls) Gorge Walk
places.note: Short half-day out of Karakol, red sandstone cliffs and a walk up the valley past Broken Heart rock toward the meadows. Distance is around 8-10km round trip if you walk to the flower valley (Valley of Flowers) turnoff, minimal elevation gain on the lower section. Good as the low-effort day if weather or legs rule out the main trek, or as a warm-up the day before.

places.name: Ala-Kul to Altyn Arashan Traverse
places.note: The reason to come to Karakol. Two to three days: trailhead near Ak-Suu (Teplokluchenka) up the Karakol valley, camp near the lake, cross the Ala-Kul pass at about 3860m, descend into Altyn Arashan. Round trip distance is roughly 45-55km depending on route and exit point, elevation gain over 1700m to the pass. Needs a tent, proper boots, and either a guide or solid navigation, the pass is unmarked scree and can hold snow into July. This is the trip, budget three full days for it including the Altyn Arashan soak at the end.

places.name: Supara Ethno Complex
places.note: Recreated traditional village outside the city with yurts and a big set menu dinner. Touristy but genuinely good food and a decent way to spend a first evening if not too jet-lagged, needs a taxi to reach.

places.name: Panfilov Park
places.note: Small amusement park with old Soviet rides still running. More about the atmosphere than the rides themselves, good with jet lag when you don't want to think.

outings.why: The high point of the trip: a 3900m pass above the turquoise Ala-Kul lake, then a long descent into the Altyn Arashan valley, hard on the knees and weather-exposed above the treeline.
outings.name: Ala-Kul to Altyn Arashan traverse, day 1: Karakol to Ala-Kul to Altyn Arashan

outings.why: A recovery day after the pass: short walks up the valley and a soak in the mineral hot springs, low effort by design.
outings.name: Altyn Arashan hot springs and valley day
outings.fallback: Just stay at the springs if the legs are done.

outings.why: The exit route back down the valley road, walkable or a rough jeep ride, back to a real bed and a shower in Karakol.
outings.name: Altyn Arashan to Karakol, jeep or walk out

destination.name: Kyrgyzstan
destination.pitch: Real high-mountain trekking without the Nepal crowds, but a 7-day trip is really four and a half usable days once you account for the flights, so pick one trek and do it properly.
destination.caveat: Flying from the US burns almost two full days each way, so a 7-day trip on paper is closer to four and a half usable days on the ground. Put together for you just now from what I know, rather than checked against today's opening times. Worth confirming anything you're pinning the trip on.

because.nature: Glacial lakes, a 3900m pass, and alpine valleys with almost no infrastructure between them.
because.adventure: The Ala-Kul to Altyn Arashan traverse is a proper high-pass trek with a night in a valley of hot springs at the end.
because.exploration: Karakol is a launchpad into terrain most travelers never bother reaching.
